Claudio Guazzoni: public comments

Claudio Guazzoni’s* Public Comments: An Ironic Lecture on Monetizing Property. After promising to speak for less than the previous speaker, Mr. McFadden, who spoke for 3 minutes and 40 seconds, Guazzoni spoke for approximately 4 minutes and 45 seconds without being cut off by the mayor. He questioned the commercial use of residential property and, in my opinion, made an apparent secondhand jab at the McFaddens, by inference, through his “trailer park” and “GoFundMe” remarks. Yet the New York Post previously reported two city enforcement actions involving short-term rental listings at his own Manhattan property. Residents can judge the consistency of his position for themselves. Read the reporting.

*Self-proclaimed public advocate.

September 17 Board meeting record

Mayor Citrin’s Board Blames Mayor Mac’s Administration for Today’s Tax Hikes

The Records Tell a Different Story.

The official agenda described a continued discussion of a proposed Village Code amendment concerning the “prohibition of rentals of non-residential structures to the general public.” Before the meeting, David and Robin McFadden submitted detailed questions for the official record. Robin then read a statement into the record during public comment.

New · September 18
Read Mayor Mac’s Response to Mayor Citrin’s Accusations Regarding Property-Tax Increases and Infrastructure September 17 Board of Trustees meeting · Response memorandum with Exhibits A through J
View the record →

During the discussion, Deputy Mayor Michele Lindsay challenged a statement I previously submitted concerning the combined effect of rising taxes, increasing debt service, appropriated reserves, continuing infrastructure needs, and broader restrictions on private-property rights:

“Taxes are rising, debt service is increasing, reserves are being appropriated, and important infrastructure needs remain. Combining those financial pressures with broader restrictions on private-property rights risks discouraging prospective buyers, narrowing the market, and placing downward pressure on property values.”

Deputy Mayor Lindsay suggested that the current Board’s infrastructure spending and property-tax increases were necessary because my administration had deferred infrastructure work or had not raised sufficient taxes to pay for it.

Trustee Joshua Scherer then stated, in substance and not as a verbatim quotation, that he had voted to lower property taxes during my administration but, based on what he knows now, regrets that vote and would instead have voted to increase taxes.

I understood their position to be that my administration’s decision not to impose larger tax increases contributed to the Village’s present financial circumstances and forced the current Board to raise residents’ property taxes.

Deputy Mayor Lindsay asked me to submit a letter stating whether I agree that those assertions are true. I will provide that written response.

I do not agree with their characterization, and I intend to respond with the underlying financial records: budgets, tax levies, debt schedules, reserve balances, capital spending, infrastructure records, and Board minutes. In other words, I will respond with receipts.

Residents should be able to evaluate the actual documents rather than competing recollections or political assertions.
